name: Karl Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent of AI firms, employers, unions, parties and government, and we don't sell or campaign. Your answers are confidential, including what you might not say in front of your team. What fills a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead four people approving local event sponsorships for a large drinks company. A youth tournament wants money for shirts, a venue wants equipment, and we check the budgets, draft agreements and book the deliveries. I've managed this desk for nine years and know the organisers, though I still need finance to catch a bad cost estimate. I have a bachelor's degree and have never used an AI tool; I prefer the signed form and a phone call.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What gives you satisfaction, and what does home look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like watching a promised set of goalposts actually arrive before a children's match. I'm 43, married to Clara, a pharmacist, and our children are eight and fourteen. We have a mortgage, but my pay is high for this role, Clara's hours are steady and we keep nine months of expenses saved. There are plenty of marketing offices nearby, though I don't want to leave a good team over a rumour. I help coach a youth football club on Saturdays, for free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some forms might fill themselves, but someone still has to check the club exists and the equipment reaches it. That's close to our current work. With Clara's wage and nine months saved, our mortgage does not feel at risk from a small software change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my team to keep signed budgets beside every sponsorship letter. I'd tell the club I can still answer the phone when a delivery is late. I wouldn't claim a form-filling tool can set up the goalposts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel secure in this job and in our bills. My team knows the local clubs, and plenty of other offices hire people who can manage budgets. I would still be annoyed if a routine form went out with the wrong amount under my name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this month I'd keep the paper sign-off for the three largest club grants and have finance check the amounts before release. Through the first year of a plateau I'd stay on this team and move 250 monthly from my salary into our mortgage reserve while Clara's hours stay steady. I wouldn't buy a new tool just to stop writing the same address twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm. The main irritation would still be chasing a delivery van on Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What goes wrong with a delivery?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week a tournament had shirts but no goalposts because the van went to another venue with the same street name. I rang the driver and the coach, then used my car to carry the bolts. A sponsorship email cannot put goalpost bolts in my car boot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep adding cash to nine months?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our older child will be looking at training or study in a few years. I don't know what it will cost yet, and I would rather have choices. I'd pause the 250 if Clara's pharmacy hours fell.

I'd tell the club I can still **answer the phone** when deliveries fail.
think: My **job and bills** feel secure while software only fills forms.
I would still mind a wrong amount going out **under my name**.
do: Keep **paper sign-off** and finance checks for the three largest grants.
Move **250 monthly** into cash while Clara's pharmacy hours stay steady.
feel: I feel **calm**, with ordinary irritation about late deliveries.
S0.quote: A sponsorship email cannot put goalpost bolts in my car boot.
fieldNote: He trusts **signed budgets** and phone calls more than an untested new tool.
High pay, Clara's wage and **nine months saved** make the plateau financially calm.

Move 250 monthly into cash only while Clara’s pharmacy hours stay steady

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing agreements, checking budgets, buying equipment and booking deliveries are most of my team's day. A stronger tool could prepare a grant in minutes while somebody still has to unload the goalposts. Our desk could lose a post or two before the venues change much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the company should publish a staffing plan before changing the desk. I'd tell the clubs we'll still check what arrives, not just what was promised. I won't say a staff cut is harmless because the forms look tidy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own job could shrink; I've done it a long time, but I am not the sharpest budget analyst. I don't use AI and I don't want to pretend I can oversee a new system after one demonstration. Clara's pay and our savings would carry us while I looked at other work, but the high salary would be hard to replace quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I'd ask for the proposed headcount and watch a trial on old sponsorship requests with a finance colleague. I'd keep calling clubs about actual deliveries and let the colleague explain any new budget checker before I touch it. If the director announces fewer posts, I'd apply for posted event-management jobs nearby only when the pay and hours are clear; I'd stay employed until a signed offer arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing the pay I have, not just a title. Our reserve helps, but I don't want to spend it while the company saves a line in its budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the budget checker after watching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if it catches a real error on old forms and the company gives me paid time to learn it properly. I have never used an AI tool. A rushed live grant is not where I want my first attempt with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a team member who wants it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd let them test it on old cases and tell me what they find. I won't punish curiosity; I just won't call a fast grant a good one until the shirts and goalposts arrive. People need work that pays, and clubs need equipment.

think: My **high-paying post** could shrink when grants become easier to write.
I don't yet know AI well enough to **oversee a live system** after one demonstration.
do: Watch an **old-case trial** with a finance colleague before judging the checker.
Keep **calling clubs** to confirm equipment arrived.
Apply for **posted event jobs** only with clear pay and hours, leaving after a signed offer.
feel: I feel **anxious** about replacing my wage, though savings buy time.
S1.quote: A rushed live grant is not where I want my first attempt with AI.
fieldNote: He will observe a **proved old-case test**, without claiming AI skill he lacks.
His **nine-month reserve** softens risk, but matching high salary quickly remains hard.
He favours actual **equipment arrival** over impressive agreement-writing speed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If full AGI can judge budgets, write agreements and decide which club gets support by 2028, it can do nearly all of my desk. Robots that move equipment arrive around 2031, but I am not paid to lift goalposts. I would have to think about income outside corporate sponsorship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team the 2028 date and ask for actual notice terms. I'd tell Clara the pharmacy wage covers our mortgage and groceries, but we still need my income for the children's costs and saving. In public I'd ask the company for paid training tied to real posts rather than a generous sounding promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my sponsorship role is likely to end by 2028. Clara's wage and nine months saved mean we would not lose our home in the first month, and several local firms might still have openings. I would be worried about a long stretch without my high pay, but I could take time to check offers instead of grabbing the first one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this month I'd ask the youth club whether it has a paid coaching vacancy and what certificate it requires, but I wouldn't stop doing the free Saturday session. I'd apply for a funded coaching course only if the club confirms a paid opening or a real pathway, the timetable fits our younger child's care and Clara agrees on pickup. If AGI arrives in 2028 and my office role ends, I'd take the club post only if its wage with Clara's covers mortgage, food and school costs; otherwise I'd use savings to search posted local roles while the children keep their usual routines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, but not cornered. Nine months in cash and a steady second wage let me make a considered choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a coaching certificate make you a professional coach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I know how to help eight-year-olds pass a ball, not how to run a whole programme. I'd need supervised hours and a club willing to pay. I won't call volunteer coaching a salary. Robots on sports fields are still later in this picture, but the club's scheduling and letters could change in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the club pay enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, and probably not at first. We'd put the actual wage next to the mortgage and school costs. If it falls short, I'd keep coaching for pleasure while looking for paid work elsewhere.

I'd tell Clara we need **paid training** tied to posts, not a vague promise.
think: Clara's wage and our **nine-month reserve** give me time to compare offers.
do: Ask the club about a **paid coaching vacancy** and required certificate now.
Apply for a **funded course** only with a confirmed path, supervised time and childcare covered.
Take a **paid club post** after 2028 only if combined wages cover family bills.
feel: I feel **anxious** about losing high pay, with time to choose.
S2.quote: I won't call volunteer coaching a salary.
fieldNote: He distinguishes **free Saturday coaching** from a real paid club vacancy.
A certificate needs **funding** plus supervised hours and childcare before it becomes a plan.
His reserve permits a search, but **club wages** may fall short of family bills.

steps.text: Apply for funded coaching course only with paid path, supervised hours and agreed childcare
Take posted paid club work only if combined wages cover mortgage, food and school costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to learn whether paid coaching is possible while sponsorship still pays. The desk faces AGI in 2031; hands-on field sessions face robots around 2034, though club booking and lesson plans could change in 2031. A club role would be a bridge if it paid enough, not a pension plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues to check real vacancies and wages before buying courses. I'd tell Clara I want to keep nine months of expenses in cash while I test the coaching route. I would still volunteer for the Saturday children even if a paid role does not appear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might work in a youth club if I earn the certificate and the pay fits, but I do not know how many posts exist. The high wage from sponsorship may continue until 2031, which lets us save more or pay down the mortgage. I cannot treat the physical field time as sheltered after robots arrive around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2027 I'd ask the club for a funded coaching certificate with paid supervised sessions and complete it only if a real trainee place is offered and Clara can cover our younger child's pickup. I'd put 350 monthly from my wage toward mortgage principal while preserving nine months of cash and covering school costs. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, I'd apply for a posted coaching or venue post only if its pay plus Clara's covers mortgage, food and school costs; otherwise I'd keep my volunteer session and search other paid openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the future wage, but five years leaves room to test. I won't sell my children a new career before a club offers one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you learn on a supervised session?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn how to manage an injured player and when to call a qualified medic, not just how to arrange a drill. A parent is trusting the coach with a child, not buying a clever lesson plan. I'd want an experienced coach beside me before taking the group alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why pay extra on the mortgage instead of investing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A smaller payment would make a lower coaching wage more plausible. I don't know which investments win in this picture. The extra 350 stops before I touch the emergency reserve or miss a school bill.

I'd tell Clara I will keep **nine months cash** while testing coaching.

My sponsorship pay could continue until 2031, letting us **reduce mortgage debt**.
do: Complete a **funded coaching certificate** only with a paid trainee place, supervision and pickup covered.
Pay **350 extra monthly** on mortgage only while nine months cash and school costs stay protected.
Apply after 2031 for **posted coaching work** only if combined wages cover family bills.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about future wages, with time to test a real route.

fieldNote: He would learn **player safety** from an experienced coach, not just lesson planning.
Mortgage prepayment is **conditional** on cash and school bills remaining covered.
He recognises **2031 desk exposure** and 2034 physical robot risk for a coaching bridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In ten years I'll be 53, our younger child eighteen and our older one twenty-four. I would like the mortgage smaller and a paid coaching option clearer by then, but neither happens just because a date is far away. Sponsorship still faces AGI in 2036, and physical field work faces robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the company to offer paid second-skill training to staff before cutting desks. I'd tell our children to learn how to work with people and equipment, not let a tool do every step. I'd tell Clara I want the mortgage numbers down before deciding whether to leave a high wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could spend years drawing a good salary, reduce the mortgage and find out whether a club would pay me. If no paid club post appears, I can still look at several local employers, though their marketing desks could face AGI too. With nine months saved and Clara's wage, I don't need to take an unfunded course out of fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2027 I'd ask for one paid venue-operations day each month through our sponsorship partners, and complete it only if the venue agrees, my company covers my time and our children’s care is covered. I'd put 400 extra monthly toward the mortgage while wages cover school costs and nine months of expenses remain saved. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, I'd take a posted physical venue role only if its wage with Clara's covers bills; if none is affordable, I'd search nearby firms while robots are still about three years away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel mostly calm. A decade and our savings give me time to choose rather than pretend a training certificate is a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do on the venue day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help set up goalposts, inspect the bolts and see how a grounds team closes a field safely. A risk form will also change with AGI in 2036, while lifting and fixing remain physical until around 2039. The venue manager would have to trust me with the work before paying me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if Clara wants to use the savings differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would decide together; the mortgage reserve belongs to our household. If one of the children needs help after school, that comes before my paid experiment. I won't trade family time for a job that is only an idea.

Unfunded courses make little sense while **cash and local options** give us time.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Sponsorship decisions and agreement writing could be done before I have a second paid skill, and other marketing offices may be cutting too. Clear notice and a real paid vacancy would help more than a course brochure. If I tried coaching for income, I'd need the required certificate, a club that pays and hours that fit our younger child's care.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the volunteer who is waiting for the promised goalposts on Saturday morning. A flawless sponsorship agreement cannot hold up a crossbar. I'd rather tell a club we are late than send them a perfect email with no equipment.

headlineQuote: A flawless sponsorship agreement cannot hold up a crossbar.
portrait: Karl, **43**, has managed four sponsorship staff for nine years at a large drinks company and coaches youth football without pay.
He has a **bachelor's degree** and ordinary skill and has never used AI; finance still catches some estimates.
He and Clara have **two school-age children** and a mortgage, with nine months saved on high pay and steady pharmacy hours.
He will consider **paid coaching** or venue work only if qualifications, actual wages and family hours fit.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his sponsorship desk before another paid skill or opening is ready.
whatWouldHelp: **Clear notice** and a real vacancy with pay that covers family bills.
A **funded coaching certificate** and paid club hours that fit childcare, if he pursues that route.
